thread.title: Trump era ignites badly needed boom in business investment

author: Jeffry Bartash
title: Trump era ignites badly needed boom in business investment
text:
Getty Images Apple and many other American companies have announced fresh plans for large U.S. investments after Congress passed the biggest corporate tax cuts in three decades. A coincidence? Overjoyed by the Trump tax cuts, a horde of companies say they plan to give more money to workers or boost investment in the United States. Is it a tipping point for a slow-growing economy or just an easy public-relations win for firms eager to earn the applause of a mercurial president?
Also read: Here’s the truth behind the PR blitz of bonuses after tax cuts 
The answer will go a long way in determining whether the U.S. economy grows significantly faster in the years ahead and raises the standard of living for Americans.
The new law reflects the most dramatic shift in how businesses are taxed since 1986. The top corporate tax rate, for example, was slashed to 21% from 35%. And a slew of related measures make it cheaper for companies to invest, especially this year.
President Trump and his Republican allies in Congress promised the tax cuts would spawn more jobs, lead to higher pay, encourage firms to locate businesses in the U.S. and speed up economic growth. 
Extremely lofty goals, all right. Is it working? The early evidence is positive —investment surged in Trump’s first year in office — but it’s still way too soon to judge, economists say.
One-winged economy More than anything else, what the economy needs right now is higher business investment. 
The economy, powered by consumer spending, has grown steadily at about 2% a year since 2010. Yet that’s well below the economy’s historic 3.2% average — and weak business investment is the biggest reason why. The economy has basically been flying with one wing.
Stronger business investment, in theory, is supposed to spawn innovation, help workers do their jobs better and increase productivity. Higher productivity in turn means companies make more profits and can afford to pay workers more. It's always been the key to a higher standard of living.
The problem is, productivity has been usually weak since the end of the 2007-2009 recession. And so have increases in worker pay. Both have grown far more slowly than normal over the past decade.
Yet investment began to surge after the election of Trump, the most pro-business president since Ronald Reagan, and the tax cuts could keep the money flowing. 
Business investment excluding housing, for instance, rose in the first three quarters of 2017 by the most in three years, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis. 
Strong business spending helped boost GDP growth above 3% in the second and third quarters and potentially the fourth quarter as well. If so, it would be the first time since 2005 the U.S. has reached 3% GDP for three quarters in a row. 
Also Read: U.S. economy primed for fast start to 2018, leading indicators show 
Another measure of business investment known as core capital orders, meanwhile, began to surge early in Trump’s first year in office. The 12-month rate of growth recently hit a five-year high of nearly 10%.
“We clearly have seen through out last year in business sentiment surveys that capital-expenditure plans have increased,” said Sam Bullard, senior economist at Wells Fargo. “A lot was on anticipation of tax cuts. I think we will see further increase in the rate of business investment.”
The broader question is whether businesses will invest enough, over a long period, to move the needle on the economy. Investment has experienced occasional surges since the end of the Great Recession, but they haven’t been sustained.
Effect of tax cuts Carl Tannenbaum, chef economist of Northern Trust, is skeptical. 
Businesses scrimped for years despite historically low interest rates, he said, suggesting they didn’t think many investments were worth it. Lower taxes rates don’t make questionable investments suddenly more attractive.
He also suspects many high-profile announcements of new investment — Apple AAPL, +0.19% and Wal-Mart WMT, +0.92% come to mind — were given great fanfare to appease Trump.
“Some of these announcements were just ratifying investments that were already in the works,” Tannenbaum asserted.
George Mokrzan, director of economics at Huntington Bancorp in Columbus Ohio, is on the other side of the fence. He argues the U.S. needed to do more after years of inaction to help American companies compete in a cutthroat global economy.
Trump Today: President says tax cuts, slashing regulations making U.S. a ‘powerhouse’ again 
“When a company makes a decision on a large investment, taxes matter,” he said. “What tax reform has done is increase long-term returns from investments. And the more investment, the more stimulus for the economy in the long run.”
Stephen Stanley, chief economist Amherst Pierpont Securities, think the tax cuts might even be a “game changer for capital investment.” He sees a boom in investment over the next few years that hopefully can drive a rebound in productivity.
“That’s been the weak spot for growth,” he said.
What might also help is the best global economy in a long time. The International Monetary Fund predicted the world will grow this year at the fastest pace since 2011 , giving businesses more reason to spend and invest.
“A lot of countries are pulling on the same side of the rope,” Bullard said.
